title: Ink-Bleed Stack — Late-Night Festival Poster
description: A concert-poster slide that floods the canvas with stacked all-caps display type — slab headline over a condensed sans support bill — sealed under a halftone grit overlay. Unlike generic bold promos, the ink-bleed texture and Hatch Show Print letterpress rhythm make every word feel hand-pressed.
philosophy: This template exists because music deserves the same visual urgency as the noise it announces. It borrows from a century of letterpress gig posters — Hatch Show Print's dense wood type, Third Man Records' deliberate rawness — and flatly refuses gradients, photography, and decorative whitespace. The speaker here is not presenting; they are billing. Every design choice narrows to a single question: does this feel like ink on paper at midnight?
goodFor: Music festival lineup announcements with 3–6 act listings
Concert or tour date reveal slides used as a single-impact opener
Brand launches targeting alternative, indie, or DIY subcultures
Event title cards where a headline and a date are the entire message
avoidFor: Chart-heavy quarterly business reviews requiring readable data labels
Healthcare or wellness presentations demanding warmth and open legibility
Multi-section decks with sustained body-copy slides
Contexts requiring WCAG accessibility compliance or low-vision readability
author: harness

examples.promptCore: This slide feels like a woodblock headline torn from a midnight press run — dense, unapologetic, and loud enough to read from across a parking lot. The compositional mood is stacked urgency: every line of type crowds the one above it, borrowing the letterpress logic of Hatch Show Print where white space is treated as waste. Texture and grain do the atmospheric heavy lifting instead of illustration or photography. Avoid any sense of digital cleanliness, spatial generosity, or decorative geometry — this should feel hand-pressed, slightly imperfect, and absolutely certain of itself.

examples.layoutNotes: Full-bleed canvas, zero outer margin — type meets every edge. A centered vertical stack divides the slide into three tight bands: the event/festival name in massive slab display occupies roughly the top 55% of the canvas height, a condensed-sans support line (date, venue, or subhead) fills the middle band at roughly half the headline cap-height, and a dense bottom strip holds tertiary billing text or a rule-and-tagline pair. No header band, no page number, no gutter breathing room — the halftone grit overlay is applied full-canvas as a final texture layer above all type.

examples.promptCore: The slide must feel like a letterpress concert bill pulled fresh off the press — dense, physical, and unapologetically loud. Compositional rhythm is stacked and modular: each listed act claims its own band, the headliner towering above tightly compressed support rows, building a cascade of visual gravity from top to bottom. A halftone grit overlay coats the full canvas so that type reads as ink absorbed into paper rather than pixels rendered on glass. Avoid any open whitespace, rounded softness, or finish that reads as digital or corporate.

examples.layoutNotes: Full-bleed canvas with a tight 4–5% outer margin — no breathing room is structural to the style. Content renders as a stacked bill: three to six horizontal band rows running edge-to-edge, each separated by a solid rule break of alternating weight. Type hierarchy is enforced by extreme size contrast: the top-billed act dominates its own oversized band, while support entries collapse into compressed, equalized rows below it. A venue/date lockup anchors bottom-left flush; page number is suppressed entirely.
